articles.title: Exclusive: SE3, a German startup building ‘spatial intelligence’ for military drones, gets $30 million in Series A funding
articles.snippet: Exclusive: SE3, a German startup building ‘spatial intelligence’ for military drones, gets $30 million in Series A funding Fortune
articles.text:
SE3, a Munich-based startup that makes AI software to help drones and other unmanned military systems understand the three-dimensional world around them, has raised $30 million in a Series A round led by Accel.
Recommended Video
Keen, Lakestar, and Seedcamp also participated in the funding round. It comes less than five months after the company, which recently dropped “Labs” from its name, emerged from stealth with €5.5 million ($6.1 million) in seed funding.
SE3’s software takes video and sensor feeds from multiple drones and ground vehicles and fuses them into a single 3D picture of the battlefield—”like a mini map, how you would know it from a strategy game,” cofounder and CEO Lukas Köstler told Fortune .
On top of that map sits a layer that labels objects and how they relate to one another, so soldiers can query it in plain language: How do I reach a target without being seen? What’s a good route for a heavy vehicle?
Operators can also give commands the same way. Rather than remotely piloting a drone with a joystick or having to tap away on a tablet, a soldier can simply say, “I need reconnaissance two kilometers in the north over the forest,” Köstler said, and a suitable drone would take off, fly the mission, and report back.
In addition to this map-level understanding of the battlefield, SE3 also builds the AI systems that sit inside the drones or other unmanned systems, giving them the ability to maneuver and navigate, even in cases where GPS is jammed, detect objects, and act as a “swarm” with other drones.
Köstler, who previously worked on Tesla’s Autopilot team and at Nvidia Research, said the most basic capability—drones locating themselves without GPS—has been delivered thousands of times and is “very robust.”
But he said the high-level fleet command AI is less mature. SE3 has contracts with Germany’s armed forces, the Bundeswehr, to develop it and has demonstrated it with them, but “there’s still much that needs to be built out over the next one or two years,” he said. The company also has contracts in Ukraine, where its technology is already deployed.
SE3 does not rely on general-purpose, large language models to understand physics or terrain. Instead, it uses classical computer vision algorithms to distill vast amounts of sensor data into a database a language model can query, and gives the model a harness equipped with a variety of conventional software tools the model can call. If the model needs a flight path, a conventional planning algorithm calculates one—avoiding mountains or enemy lines of sight, for example.
Simply feeding raw data to the model “wouldn’t work at all,” Köstler said. Actions such as a drone takeoff can be set to require a human operator’s approval. The system can run entirely offline, and customers can swap in their own preferred frontier AI model to act as the “brains” of the system.
SE3 spun out of the computer vision lab of Daniel Cremers at the Technical University of Munich (TUM), where Köstler and SE3’s CTO, Simon Klenk, were PhD students. Cremers serves as SE3’s chief science officer.
Military work has long made some AI researchers uneasy—a tension highlighted when the Pentagon designated Anthropic a supply-chain risk in March after it refused to let its models be used for fully autonomous weapons or mass domestic surveillance.

Ex-Tesla Engineer’s SE3 Raises $30M for Drone AI Built for Any Drone
Posted on November 13, 2026 November 12, 2026 by Flavia Moura
13
Nov
The Munich startup is the only serious bidder for the battlefield command screen that sells nothing underneath it. Ukraine approved a new drone model about every 10 hours this year. That is the whole pitch, and the whole problem.
SE3, a Munich spinout from the Technical University of Munich, raised a $30 million Series A led by Accel to build AI that runs drones from any manufacturer. The bet is that militaries will pay for neutrality as their fleets splinter. Ukraine codified 650 new drone systems in the first 265 days of 2026.
Picture a Bundeswehr operator in 2028. Her unit flies quadcopters from one German startup, fixed-wing scouts from another, loitering munitions from a third, and a couple of ground robots nobody remembers ordering. Each one shipped with its own app. Now she wants to say, out loud, “send something to look two kilometers north over that forest,” and have the right machine take off.
That sentence is the product SE3 is selling. The hard part is not the voice command. It is that the machine she wants could have been built by anyone.
What Happened
Fortune reported on November 12 that SE3, which recently dropped “Labs” from its name, closed a $30 million Series A led by Accel, with Keen, Lakestar and Seedcamp joining. Valuation, revenue and total funding were not disclosed.
The round lands fast. SE3 came out of stealth on June 26, 2026, with a €5.5 million seed (about $6.1 million) led by Lakestar, alongside Seedcamp, EWOR, the Sequoia Scout Fund and Plug and Play. That is roughly 4.9 times the seed check, raised 139 days later.
The basics:
Who: CEO Lukas Köstler, a former TUM PhD student who worked on Tesla’s Autopilot team and at Nvidia Research; CTO Simon Klenk, his TUM labmate; and chief science officer Daniel Cremers, who runs the computer vision lab the company spun out of.
What it builds: software that fuses video and sensor feeds from many drones and ground vehicles into one 3D map, labels what is in it, and lets soldiers query it or task machines by voice. It also builds onboard autonomy for navigation when GPS is jammed, object detection and swarm behavior.
Who pays: the Bundeswehr, under contracts to develop fleet command AI, plus Ukraine, where the technology is already deployed. Partners include sensor maker Hensoldt, drone software company Auterion and drone developer ERC.
What the money buys: headcount goes from about 40 to about 120, with new offices in London, Berlin, the Nordics and Baltics, and Poland.
Köstler described the shared map to Fortune as working “like a mini map, how you would know it from a strategy game.” Gamers will get it instantly. Procurement officers will get it the moment they price what happens when that mini map only shows one vendor’s units.
The Backstory
Every outlet will frame this as another European defense AI round riding rearmament money. True, and not very useful. The more interesting fact is the market structure SE3 is walking into.
Start with Ukraine, the world’s largest live test of drone procurement. Its Ministry of Defence codified 413 unmanned aerial systems in the first half of 2026, up more than 30% on the same period of 2025 and more than 73% on 2024. By September 22 the count was 650. articles.title: Spatial Intelligence Startup SE3 Raises $30M Series A Led by Accel
articles.snippet: Spatial Intelligence Startup SE3 Raises $30M Series A Led by Accel Wowtale
articles.text:
In a war zone where drones fly in large fleets, human operators cannot supervise every vehicle. When electronic warfare cuts off satellite navigation, each machine has to work out where it is and what surrounds it on its own. The EU aims to mobilise €800 billion in defence spending by 2030 and is planning a European Drone Wall to defend its eastern flank, which makes that kind of autonomy more valuable. A Munich startup working on this spatial awareness problem has raised a Series A.
SE3 combines computer vision and AI to turn sensor data into three-dimensional understanding so machines can decide and move on their own. It is developing the technology for environments where systems must keep working when satellite navigation is disrupted, and its immediate market is European defence.
The product is a spatial intelligence software layer for unmanned systems. It connects drones and ground vehicles from different manufacturers and fuses their sensor data into a shared 3D picture of the environment. It then adjusts behaviour, routes and positions for each vehicle in a swarm, and operators can command all functions by voice. The software runs entirely on the edge, so systems keep operating in contested environments.
SE3 also stresses that it is not tied to any one manufacturer’s vehicles. Modular procurement approaches such as MOSA and Germany’s MOSABw programme are making it easier for armed forces to combine systems from different suppliers, and the company sees growing demand for independent software that works across platforms without competing with the vehicles themselves.
In the past two years, SE3 has shipped thousands of systems, and it is working on multiple contracts with Ukraine and Germany’s armed forces, the Bundeswehr. It is an AI partner to defence primes including Rheinmetall and HENSOLDT and to scale-ups such as Auterion and ERC System. Auterion CEO Lorenz Meier said SE3’s spatial intelligence runs on Auterion’s Skynode, so customers get the capability on platforms they already operate, regardless of manufacturer.
SE3 spun out of the computer vision lab of Professor Daniel Cremers at the Technical University of Munich (TUM). Lukas Köstler is CEO and co-founder, and Simon Klenk is CTO. Both worked on PhDs in computer vision and robotics in that lab. Cremers is chief science officer, holds TUM’s chair for computer vision and AI, and won the Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz Prize, Germany’s most prestigious research award.
SE3 announced the $30 million Series A on November 12. Accel led the round, with Keen , Lakestar and Seedcamp participating. Accel partner Matt Robinson said a team with talent from one of Europe’s leading research departments is well placed to build spatial AI for autonomous systems, a problem defence primes have found difficult.
The company will use the funds to grow its engineering, commercial and operations teams and fulfil further contracts. It plans to strengthen its presence in Germany and Ukraine, open a UK office and expand across Europe. Defence remains the focus, with robotics, emergency response and other civilian uses to be explored from 2027.
Capital Keeps Flowing to European Defence Startups
European defence startups have been raising large rounds. Helsing , Europe’s largest defence AI company, raised $1.8 billion in a Series E at an $18 billion valuation. Anaergia: C$30 Million Credit Facility Expansion With National Bank Of Canada Increases Financing Capacity By 50%
By Amit Chowdhry
Yesterday at 4:47 PM
Anaergia: C$30 Million Credit Facility Expansion With National Bank Of Canada Increases Financing Capacity By 50%
Anaergia, a global technology company specializing in renewable natural gas and organic waste conversion, has expanded its revolving credit facility with National Bank of Canada by 50%, increasing its maximum borrowing capacity from C$20 million to C$30 million. The additional C$10 million in potential financing capacity will support the company’s working capital requirements as it executes its contracted project backlog and converts existing orders into revenue.
The amended agreement builds on the revolving credit facility originally announced on May 6, 2026.
The expansion provides Anaergia with additional financial flexibility to manage the expenditures associated with delivering renewable energy and waste management projects.
The amount available for borrowing at any particular time will remain subject to the facility’s borrowing base and other terms of the credit agreement.
Consequently, the increase in the maximum facility size does not necessarily mean that the entire C$30 million is immediately available for withdrawal.
Amounts borrowed under the facility may be used for general corporate purposes, subject to the agreement’s provisions.
Supporting Project Execution And Working Capital
Anaergia develops and delivers technologies that convert organic waste into valuable products, including renewable natural gas, fertilizer, and water.
Its business encompasses project design, equipment supply, construction, and operational services.
These projects can involve substantial engineering and equipment requirements, creating working capital needs throughout development and implementation.
The expanded credit facility is intended to support these requirements as Anaergia advances its contracted project portfolio.
Working capital is particularly important for businesses delivering large infrastructure and industrial technology projects because expenditures for materials, equipment, labor, and other activities may occur before customers make corresponding payments.
Revolving credit arrangements provide access to financing that can be drawn and repaid as needed, within the limitations of the applicable agreement.
By increasing its maximum borrowing capacity, Anaergia is seeking to improve its ability to manage project-related cash requirements.
Management identified the conversion of its contracted backlog into recognized revenue as a central operating priority.
The additional financing capacity is intended to support that objective while allowing the company to continue its focus on disciplined project execution.
Expanding Renewable Natural Gas And Waste Conversion Infrastructure
Anaergia provides integrated solutions designed to help municipalities, utilities, and industrial organizations manage organic waste more effectively.
Its technologies convert waste streams into renewable energy and other reusable products.
Renewable natural gas is commonly produced by processing biogas generated from the decomposition of organic materials.
After treatment and upgrading, the resulting gas can be used as an energy source in applications that would otherwise rely on conventional natural gas.
Anaergia also develops solutions that recover useful materials from waste processing operations.
